item.title: Kayzia takes the stage
item.description: For Kayzia, this Saturday’s VT1S concert will be the biggest stage she’s ever been on. She’ll be performing three songs live for the first time.
item.content:encoded:
For Kayzia, this Saturday’s VT1S concert will be the biggest stage she’s ever been on.

She’ll be performing three songs live for the first time.

“For me, it’s a big thing because it’s my first time performing on stage,” she said.

“And the only time I’ve been singing was in church. So, this is going to be my first time performing my three songs on stage.”

She’s feeling both nervous and excitement as rehearsals ramp up with her team.

“I’m feeling nervous and excited too. Just practising, doing rehearsals.”

For Kayzia, going from singing in church to a festival crowd is a huge step.

She’s inviting everyone to come support and experience it with her.

item.title: BSP announces major leadership restructure in Fiji
item.description: BSP Financial Group has announced a major leadership restructuring aimed at strengthening its regional operations and succession planning. Michael Nacola, who has served as the Managing Director of BSP Life in Fiji for the past seven years, will step into the newly created role of Deputy Country Head for BSP Fiji.
item.content:encoded:
BSP Financial Group has announced a major leadership restructuring aimed at strengthening its regional operations and succession planning.

Michael Nacola, who has served as the Managing Director of BSP Life in Fiji for the past seven years, will step into the newly created role of Deputy Country Head for BSP Fiji.

He will report directly to BSP Fiji Country Head, Haroon Ali.

Mr Nacola will officially assume his new responsibilities once a successor is appointed at BSP Life.

A comprehensive internal and external search is currently underway to fill his vacant position.

In tandem with this appointment, Maikash Ali’s leadership portfolio has been expanded.

In addition to his current duties as Head of Corporate and Institutional Banking for Fiji, he has been promoted to Regional Head of Corporate and Institutional Banking.

item.title: Family members urged to share RHD burden
item.description: Caring for children living with rheumatic heart disease should not be a burden carried by mothers alone, says Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran. She made the comment while launching World Heart Month 2026 at the Grand Pacific Hotel as part of a global campaign to raise awareness on cardiovascular disease.
item.content:encoded:
Caring for children living with rheumatic heart disease should not be a burden carried by mothers alone, says Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection Sashi Kiran.

She made the comment while launching World Heart Month 2026 at the Grand Pacific Hotel as part of a global campaign to raise awareness on cardiovascular disease.

“Fathers, grandparents, guardians and extended family members all have a critical role to play in lifting this burden,” she said.

Ms Kiran urged parents and caregivers to take symptoms such as persistent sore throats and painful joints seriously and seek medical attention early.

She also called on people to regularly check their blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol to reduce the risk of heart disease and stroke.

“Every heartbeat matters. Each of us has a profound responsibility to protect our own health and the health of those we care for.”

Ms Kiran said financial hardship, transport difficulties, poor housing and limited access to services could prevent families from maintaining treatment.

The theme for World Heart Month 2026 is “Don’t miss a beat”.

item.title: Reconciliation identifies 61 cases for investigation
item.description: A TOTAL of 61 online-safety cases have been referred to the authorities for investigation, prompting the Online Safety Commission and police to strengthen the way serious complaints are tracked and progressed. Online Safety Commissioner Filipe Batiwale said victims needed greater certainty about their cases after they were referred for criminal investigation.
item.content:encoded:
A TOTAL of 61 online-safety cases have been referred to the authorities for investigation, prompting the Online Safety Commission and police to strengthen the way serious complaints are tracked and progressed.

Online Safety Commissioner Filipe Batiwale said victims needed greater certainty about their cases after they were referred for criminal investigation.

A recent reconciliation exercise between the two agencies identified 61 cases referred by the commission to the police.

Mr Batiwale said the two departments were working to improve the acknowledgement, tracking and progression of referrals and the sharing of case-status information.

“When someone comes to us, tells us what has happened, provides the material and goes through the complaint process, they understandably want to know what happens next,” he said.

“If we refer that matter for criminal investigation, OSC and police both need a clear system that allows the case to be tracked and, where appropriate, allows the complainant to be told where things stand.”

He said the issue was not about blaming either institution, but ensuring their respective roles worked effectively together.

“Police have a very large mandate. They deal with every type of crime in Fiji. OSC has a specialist mandate.

“We need to make sure those two roles work together properly instead of creating unnecessary duplication.”

Mr Batiwale said serious online complaints could involve children, intimate images, threats, exploitation, fake accounts and digital evidence that could disappear quickly.

item.title: Writers move to close iTaukei book gap
item.description: A LONGSTANDING shortage of iTaukei reading material is leaving children with too few books in their own language, prompting writers, educators and illustrators to work together to close the gap. The three-day inaugural Talanoa Booklab workshop at the Centre for Appropriate Technology and Development conference centre in Nadave, Tailevu, this week focused on developing and finalising iTaukei short
item.content:encoded:
A LONGSTANDING shortage of iTaukei reading material is leaving children with too few books in their own language, prompting writers, educators and illustrators to work together to close the gap.

The three-day inaugural Talanoa Booklab workshop at the Centre for Appropriate Technology and Development conference centre in Nadave, Tailevu, this week focused on developing and finalising iTaukei short stories for Years 7 and 8 students.

University of the South Pacific linguistics and Fijian studies lecturer Apolonia Tamata said the lack of resources had persisted for years, with few iTaukei books available for children, particularly short stories and poetry.

“The gap in iTaukei literacy hasn’t been met and has been an issue over the years,” she said.

Ms Tamata said the shortage also threatened the preservation of iTaukei stories, many of which had traditionally been passed down orally without being documented.

The project, in partnership with the Ministry of Education’s curriculum advisory services, aims to develop fiction, non-fiction and other iTaukei stories for the national curriculum.

Ms Tamata said this was the first time iTaukei writers had come together to develop curriculum-based short stories.

Writers and editors are working through talanoa sessions to refine the material, with Ms Tamata and her team ensuring the stories meet linguistic and educational standards.

She said the project was about more than producing textbooks — it was about ensuring iTaukei children could see their language, culture and stories reflected in what they read.

“We hope that every iTaukei child out there knows that they have iTaukei books published for them,” she said.

item.title: National airline turns 75
item.description: FIJI Airways is celebrating 75 years of connecting Fiji to the world, marking a journey that began with a seven-seat de Havilland Dragon Rapide flying from Nausori to Drasa, near Lautoka, on September 1, 1951. Founded by aviation pioneer Harold Gatty, the airline was renamed Air Pacific in 1970 before reclaiming its original name, Fiji Airways, in 2013.
item.content:encoded:
FIJI Airways is celebrating 75 years of connecting Fiji to the world, marking a journey that began with a seven-seat de Havilland Dragon Rapide flying from Nausori to Drasa, near Lautoka, on September 1, 1951.

Founded by aviation pioneer Harold Gatty, the airline was renamed Air Pacific in 1970 before reclaiming its original name, Fiji Airways, in 2013.

Today, Fiji Airways operates a fleet of 23 aircraft, connects Fiji directly to 37 destinations across 14 countries and provides access to more than 900 destinations through its membership of the oneworld alliance.

The airline carries about 70 per cent of visitors who fly to Fiji and employs more than 2000 people across the group.

Airline managing director and chief executive officer Paul Scurrah said the 75th anniversary was an opportunity to recognise the thousands of Fijians who had contributed to the airline’s growth and the millions of customers who had travelled with Fiji Airways.

“From a seven-seat aircraft flying between two small airstrips to a global oneworld carrier flying to 900-plus destinations, we’re still doing what we set out to do in 1951, connecting Fiji to the people and places that matter most,” Mr Scurrah said.

The airline is marking the anniversary with an eight-day sale from September 1 to 8, offering special fares across selected destinations.

Fiji Airways said the milestone represented more than the anniversary of an airline, but 75 years of journeys, people and Fiji’s connection with the world.

item.title: ‘Homes lacked basic facility’
item.description: TWO basic facilities were missing from some homes when Vunidogoloa villagers in Cakaudrove were relocated in 2014, forcing the community to build their own kitchens and improve toilet facilities. Village headman Apimeleki Qiliho said the relocation was part of a project by the former government to move the community away from rising sea levels and the impacts of climate change.
item.content:encoded:
TWO basic facilities were missing from some homes when Vunidogoloa villagers in Cakaudrove were relocated in 2014, forcing the community to build their own kitchens and improve toilet facilities.

Village headman Apimeleki Qiliho said the relocation was part of a project by the former government to move the community away from rising sea levels and the impacts of climate change.

The project cost millions of dollars and was jointly funded by the FijiFirst government and the village’s own logging resources.

Mr Qiliho said villagers were grateful for the assistance, but some essential facilities were not included in the new homes.

“We had to build our own kitchens because the homes that were built did not have one,” he said.

He said some houses also lacked proper toilet facilities.

“We made history in January 2014 as the first village in Fiji to undergo a government-planned relocation because of rising sea levels. Seawater regularly reached people’s doorsteps,” he said.

“More than 130 villagers moved about two kilometres uphill to a new site they named Kenani, the new village site. There were no other options for us. We had to move,” he said.

Mr Qiliho said the experience highlighted the need to ensure basic household facilities were included in future relocation projects.

item.title: $2.8b injection | Tourism remains Fiji’s largest industry and private employer
item.description: TOURISM remains Fiji’s largest industry and private employer, contributing $2.81 billion to the economy from a record 986,367 visitor arrivals in 2025. Deputy Prime Minister Viliame Gavoka revealed these statistics at the opening of the Pacific Polytech Melrose Hotel in Sigatoka early this week, saying the record performance demonstrated the importance of maintaining a skilled workforce to support
item.content:encoded:
TOURISM remains Fiji’s largest industry and private employer, contributing $2.81 billion to the economy from a record 986,367 visitor arrivals in 2025.

Deputy Prime Minister Viliame Gavoka revealed these statistics at the opening of the Pacific Polytech Melrose Hotel in Sigatoka early this week, saying the record performance demonstrated the importance of maintaining a skilled workforce to support the sector’s continued growth.

“The Fiji Bureau of Statistics tells us that in 2025, our country welcomed a record 986,367 visitors, and that tourism earned Fiji $2.81b,” Mr Gavoka said.

“This is our largest industry and our largest private employer.”

Mr Gavoka said tourism also provided employment opportunities for people in rural and coastal communities, allowing young people to find work without leaving their home areas.

He said tourism was central to the National Development Plan 2025-2029 and Vision 2050, with the National Sustainable Tourism Framework 2024-2034 setting the direction for the sector.

The framework focuses on four goals — a prosperous visitor economy, thriving and inclusive communities, cultures that are seen and valued, and healthy islands and oceans.

“People sit inside every one of them. There is no prosperous visitor economy without a trained workforce, and this is where Pacific Polytech becomes essential to national policy.”

He said the Government was also modernising the legislation governing the tourism industry.

“For too long, our industry ran on world-class beauty and warm hospitality, but on a legal foundation that was scattered and dated.

Mr Gavoka said the Tourism Act 2026, enacted in June, provided the industry with a single modern legal framework.

He also highlighted Parliament’s passage of the Commercial Use of Marine Areas reforms, known as CUMA, which returns proprietary ownership of commercial marine areas to the relevant iTaukei customary owners.

He said the reform would modernise the management of marine areas used for tourism while ensuring customary owners benefited from the resources attracting visitors to Fiji.

“The reef and the lagoon that draw the world to our shores will work for the communities that have always belonged to them.”

Mr Gavoka said tourism growth also depended on a reliable and safe aviation sector.

He said Government had released the Civil Aviation Master Plan for Fiji 2026-2031 and is developing a new Civil Aviation Bill to consolidate aviation laws under a single modern Act.

“Clear law and safe skies are what keep the aircraft coming, and the visitors with them.”
